title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Tensor Parallelism
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: In the previous part, we explored why a single GPU is often not enough. Sometimes the model itself does not fit into memory. Other times, even if it fits, one GPU cannot handle enough concurrent users.
That naturally leads to the next question. How do we actually use multiple GPUs?
One important idea here is tensor parallelism. But before understanding tensor parallelism, it helps to first understand what a tensor actually is.
What is a tensor?
The word sounds complicated, but the idea is actually simple. A tensor is just a way of organizing numbers.
Depending on how numbers are arranged, we give them different names.
A single number is called a scalar.
Example:
A list of numbers is called a vector.
Example:
A table of numbers with rows and columns is called a matrix.
Example:
A tensor is the general term that includes all of these.
So:

scalar → 0D tensor
vector → 1D tensor
matrix → 2D tensor
Anything with more dimensions is also called a tensor.
Why do tensors matter in LLMs?
LLMs operate almost entirely on tensors.
Words become numbers. Those numbers are arranged into vectors and matrices. Then the model continuously transforms these tensors during computation.
For example:

embeddings are tensors
activations are tensors
KV cache stores tensors
weights are tensors
Almost everything inside the model is represented this way.
What do weights look like?
Earlier, we discussed parameters and weights. These weights are usually stored as matrices.
For example:
That means:

4096 rows
4096 columns
millions of numbers inside one tensor
The model performs operations on these tensors repeatedly during inference.
Why do we need tensor parallelism?
Suppose we have a very large model.
Inside the model, we may have weight matrices like:
That is roughly:
≈ 16 million parameters
And this is just one matrix.
A full model contains many such matrices across many layers. Eventually, the model becomes too large for one GPU.
So the natural idea becomes:
Can we split these tensors across GPUs?
This leads to tensor parallelism.
What does splitting a tensor mean?
Suppose we have a matrix like this:

[
 [ W W W W ]
 [ W W W W ]
 [ W W W W ]
 [ W W W W ]
]
Normally, one GPU stores the entire matrix.
With tensor parallelism, we divide the matrix across GPUs.
For example:

GPU 1:
[
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
]

GPU 2:
[
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
]
Now each GPU stores only part of the weights.
What happens during computation?
Suppose an input arrives.
Example:
Input → [ x1 x2 x3 x4 ]
Normally:

one GPU multiplies the full input with the full weight matrix
and produces the output
With tensor parallelism:

the same input is sent to multiple GPUs
each GPU computes using only its portion of the weights
Example:

GPU 1 → partial computation
GPU 2 → partial computation
Each GPU produces part of the result. These partial results are then combined together.
What does this achieve?
Instead of one GPU handling the entire model, we now distribute the model across GPUs.
This helps in two ways:

the model fits into memory
computation is shared across GPUs
Large models that previously could not run on one GPU now become possible.
Is the computation completely independent?
Not really.
After each GPU computes its partial result:

outputs must be combined
GPUs must synchronize
data must move between GPUs
So tensor parallelism introduces communication between GPUs.
Why is communication important?
If GPUs constantly exchange data:

latency increases
synchronization overhead increases
bandwidth becomes important
So tensor parallelism is always a tradeoff:

better memory scaling
but more communication cost
Does tensor parallelism help with concurrent users?
Not directly.
The main goal of tensor parallelism is to make large models fit across GPUs.
In some cases, distributing weights across GPUs can free up memory for:

larger KV cache
larger batches
more active requests
So it can indirectly improve concurrency.
But scaling to many users is usually solved differently. We will come back to that later.
What does this feel like intuitively?
Imagine solving a large math problem.
Without tensor parallelism:
One person solves the entire problem
With tensor parallelism:

Multiple people solve different parts
Then combine answers
That is essentially what the GPUs are doing.
What is the key idea?
Tensor parallelism does not split users. It does not split requests. It splits the tensors themselves.
Multiple GPUs collaborate to compute a single layer of the model.
What comes next?
Tensor parallelism helps when the model itself is too large.
But there is another way to split work across GPUs.
Instead of splitting tensors inside a layer, we can split the layers themselves.
This leads to pipeline parallelism.
